sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: On-policy distillation (OPD) is the dominant paradigm for transferring reasoning capabilities from large models to smaller ones ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . It trains students on their own generated states under token-level supervision from a frozen teacher, reducing the training–inference distribution mismatch. A teacher improved through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , should therefore provide stronger supervision. Prior work indeed shows that a GRPO-trained teacher produces a stronger student than the original teacher ( Xu et al., 2026b ) . Yet our initial observations on MATH ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) show that student gains can fall short of the teacher’s GRPO improvement. We call this shortfall the transfer gap and ask: which teacher improvements transfer to the student, which do not, and how can more of them be made to transfer? Our problem-level analysis on MATH shows that this gap is not uniform across training problems (Figure 1 ). Whether a teacher improvement can transfer depends on how the GRPO-trained teacher (hereafter, the GRPO teacher ) and student perform on each problem. Where the teacher outperforms the student, two distinct learning needs arise. If the student never solves the problem, it faces a knowledge gap : it needs guidance toward correct choices it has never explored, yet standard OPD supervises only its own responses, making such gains especially difficult to transfer. If the student solves the problem only sometimes, it faces a precision gap : it needs targeted correction of specific bad choices, whereas indiscriminate distillation may transfer only part of the gain or suppress correct behavior already acquired. Conversely, when the GRPO teacher does not outperform the student, it has little improvement to transfer. When their performance is comparable or both fail, the teacher offers no better direction; when the student is stronger, matching the teacher may be harmful. Standard OPD nevertheless supervises these problems uniformly. Skipping them concentrates the training budget on problems where transfer is possible. Left: GRPO yields a teacher improvement Δ ​ T \Delta T , but standard OPD transfers only part of it into a student gain Δ ​ S \Delta S , leaving a transfer gap of Δ ​ T − Δ ​ S \Delta T-\Delta S . Middle: Joint teacher–student pass rates identify knowledge gaps (teacher > 0 >0 , student = 0 =0 ), precision gaps (teacher > > student > 0 >0 ), and problems with no transferable teacher advantage (teacher ≤ \leq student). Right: TS-OPD routes these three strata to matched actions—discover, refine, and skip, respectively. Existing OPD methods adapt supervision at the problem or token level ( Lin et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026c ; Xu et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Most closely related, Sparse-to-Dense distills from a GRPO-improved teacher using a common pipeline across problems ( Xu et al., 2026b ) . In contrast, we use the joint success of the teacher and raw student to identify each problem’s learning need and match both its KL direction and token-level supervision. We therefore propose Transfer-Stratified On-Policy Distillation (TS-OPD) . It first stratifies problems by the joint pass rates of the GRPO teacher and student, then routes knowledge and precision gaps to matched objectives with stratum-specific token gating, skipping problems without a teacher advantage. We evaluate TS-OPD across two teacher lineages (Qwen3-8B before and after GRPO), three student scales (0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B), four distillation objectives, and teacher-free direct GRPO. Our contributions are as follows: 1. We characterize and decompose the transfer gap in distillation from GRPO-improved teachers into distinct problem-level learning needs. 2. We propose TS-OPD , which stratifies and selects problems by observed teacher–student success, routes distillation objectives, and gates token-level supervision to address knowledge and precision gaps. 3. Experiments with a GRPO-improved teacher show that TS-OPD achieves the highest macro-average correctness and smallest benchmark-averaged transfer gap among evaluated methods at all three student scales, while distilling only on selected problems.

sections.heading: RL-improved teachers.
sections.text: DeepSeek-R1 distills an RL-trained model by fine-tuning on its responses ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . Sparse-to-Dense ( Xu et al., 2026b ) applies GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) to a larger teacher, then a forward-KL warmup and reverse-KL OPD uniformly across problems, and shows that the RL-improved teacher yields a student stronger than direct GRPO; it compares final students, not how much of the teacher’s GRPO gain is inherited, or where. Direct-OPD instead transfers the RL-induced policy shift, using the post-RL to pre-RL teacher log-ratio as a dense reward ( Feng et al., 2026 ) , while Li et al. (2026) find that OPD requires compatible thinking patterns and teacher capabilities new to the student ( Li et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: On-policy objectives.
sections.text: GKD trains the student on its own samples and admits divergences beyond forward KL ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , and MiniLLM optimizes reverse KL on-policy ( Gu et al., 2024 ) . AKL, ToDi, EOPD, and TrOPD combine forward and reverse KL through adaptive weights, per-token probability ratios, teacher entropy, or token-level trust regions ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Jung et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2026 ; Xing et al., 2026 ) ; none chooses the direction from per-problem teacher and student performance ( Ko et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) .

sections.heading: Selective distillation.
sections.text: PACED weights each problem by p ⁡ ( 1 − p ) p(1-p) of the student pass rate p p and applies a forward-then-reverse KL schedule to all problems ( Xu et al., 2026a ) ; TREK applies forward KL on verified teacher proposals for prompts the student rarely solves, then returns to GRPO ( Xu et al., 2026d ; Yan et al., 2025 ) ; TGOPD routes each prompt to OPD or GRPO using verifier-scored teacher probes ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Within responses, OPDVR gates the distillation reward by trajectory correctness ( Lin et al., 2026 ) , and TIP selects tokens by student entropy and teacher–student divergence ( Xu et al., 2026c ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . Unlike these student-only or teacher-only signals, TS-OPD uses the joint success of the GRPO teacher and the raw student to choose each problem’s KL direction (forward for knowledge gaps, reverse for precision gaps) and adds response-local token gating, rather than introducing problem-level selection itself.

sections.heading: 3  Problem Definition and Transfer-Gap Diagnosis
sections.text: Building on our observations on MATH, we formalize the transfer gap and identify knowledge and precision gaps on MATH training problems. We examine these strata alongside gain shortfalls on held-out competition benchmarks to motivate differentiated OPD supervision.

sections.heading: 3.2  Two Learning Gaps on Training Problems
sections.text: We hypothesize that incomplete transfer partly reflects supervision mismatched to problem-specific learning needs . A stronger teacher need not outperform the student on every problem. Where it does, the guidance needed depends on whether the student can already generate a correct response. Before distillation, we therefore sample K cal = 8 K_{\mathrm{cal}}=8 responses per training problem from both T 1 T_{1} and S 0 S_{0} and classify their joint success rates. A: knowledge gap , p ^ S 0 , i = 0 < p ^ T 1 , i \widehat{p}_{S_{0},i}=0<\widehat{p}_{T_{1},i} . The student needs to discover correct choices absent from its sampled rollouts, not merely increase the frequency of existing correct responses. Zero observed success at a finite budget does not imply zero ability. C: precision gap , 0 < p ^ S 0 , i < p ^ T 1 , i 0<\widehat{p}_{S_{0},i}<\widehat{p}_{T_{1},i} . The student already produces correct responses but less reliably, calling for targeted correction while preserving existing correct behavior. P: student advantage , p ^ S 0 , i > p ^ T 1 , i \widehat{p}_{S_{0},i}>\widehat{p}_{T_{1},i} ; N: no observed gap , equal rates, including joint failures. Neither shows an observed teacher advantage, so neither is prioritized for distillation. Let 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} be the training-problem index set, with subsets 𝒟 A \mathcal{D}_{A} and 𝒟 C \mathcal{D}_{C} for the knowledge and precision gaps. Using | ⋅ | |\cdot| for set cardinality and 𝟏 ​ [ ⋅ ] \mathbf{1}[\cdot] for the indicator function, define the teacher-advantage problem fraction : r adv = | 𝒟 A | + | 𝒟 C | | 𝒟 train | = 1 | 𝒟 train | ∑ i ∈ 𝒟 train 𝟏 [ p ^ T 1 , i > p ^ S 0 , i ] . r_{\mathrm{adv}}=\frac{|\mathcal{D}_{A}|+|\mathcal{D}_{C}|}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}|}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}}\mathbf{1}[\widehat{p}_{T_{1},i}>\widehat{p}_{S_{0},i}]. (3) This is the fraction of problems with an observed teacher advantage before training, not its magnitude. All four stratum fractions use the full training set as the denominator and sum to one.

sections.heading: 3.4  Implications for OPD Supervision
sections.text: For A, correct responses may be rare in student rollouts. Because OPD queries the teacher along student-generated prefixes ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) , guidance along complete correct solutions may be limited. Feedback at incorrect prefixes remains available but may not suffice to reach a correct solution, motivating guidance toward teacher-preferred continuations the student rarely selects. For C, uniform supervision may miss decisive errors and spend limited budget on P and N, leaving learnable problems undertrained. This motivates targeted correction while preserving existing correct behavior. These mechanism hypotheses require fixed-budget stratification controls and token-level analysis. We therefore prioritize A and C with supervision matched to knowledge acquisition and precision improvement, deferring teacher matching on P and N. Strata are assigned before training from joint teacher–student samples; rollouts remain student-generated.

sections.heading: 4  Transfer-Stratified On-Policy Distillation
sections.text: TS-OPD labels training problems by the teacher and student success observed before training and works at two levels (Figure 2 ). At the problem level , it trains only on A and C problems ( filtering ) and applies forward KL to A and reverse KL to C ( routing ). At the token level , it updates only selected positions within each response and adds an entropy brake on C ( gating ). TS-OPD (routing only) keeps the problem level and drops the token level; TS-OPD uses both. Figure 2: Overview of TS-OPD. Before training, each problem is labeled by the sampled success of the teacher and the student. Problem level: P and N problems are skipped, A problems use forward KL, and C problems use reverse KL. Token level: gates select positions within a response, and C adds an entropy brake.

sections.heading: Strata.
sections.text: We use the labels 𝒟 A \mathcal{D}_{A} and 𝒟 C \mathcal{D}_{C} from Section 3, computed once per teacher–student pair from K cal = 8 K_{\mathrm{cal}}=8 samples of T 1 T_{1} and S 0 S_{0} and fixed during training. Filtering keeps only 𝒟 + = 𝒟 A ∪ 𝒟 C \mathcal{D}_{+}=\mathcal{D}_{A}\cup\mathcal{D}_{C} .

sections.heading: Notation.
sections.text: For a training problem x x , the student generates a response y = ( y 1 , … , y | y | ) y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{|y|}) of length | y | |y| . The prefix before the t t -th token is s t = ( x , y 1 , … , y t − 1 ) s_{t}=(x,y_{1},\ldots,y_{t-1}) . At s t s_{t} , the student and the teacher ( T 1 T_{1} ) assign next-token probabilities π S ​ ( v ∣ s t ) \pi_{S}(v\mid s_{t}) and π T ​ ( v ∣ s t ) \pi_{T}(v\mid s_{t}) to each token v v in the vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . OPD pulls π S \pi_{S} toward π T \pi_{T} on these prefixes ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Why forward KL for A and reverse KL for C.
sections.text: At one position (we drop s t s_{t} ), reverse KL is D R = ∑ v π S ​ ( v ) ​ log ⁡ π S ​ ( v ) π T ​ ( v ) D_{\mathrm{R}}=\sum_{v}\pi_{S}(v)\log\frac{\pi_{S}(v)}{\pi_{T}(v)} and forward KL is D F = ∑ v π T ​ ( v ) ​ log ⁡ π T ​ ( v ) π S ​ ( v ) D_{\mathrm{F}}=\sum_{v}\pi_{T}(v)\log\frac{\pi_{T}(v)}{\pi_{S}(v)} . Let z v z_{v} be the student’s logit for token v v , so π S = softmax ⁡ ( z ) \pi_{S}=\mathrm{softmax}(z) . The gradients are ∂ D R ∂ z v = π S ​ ( v ) ​ ( log ⁡ π S ​ ( v ) π T ​ ( v ) − D R ) , ∂ D F ∂ z v = π S ​ ( v ) − π T ​ ( v ) . \frac{\partial D_{\mathrm{R}}}{\partial z_{v}}=\pi_{S}(v)\Bigl(\log\frac{\pi_{S}(v)}{\pi_{T}(v)}-D_{\mathrm{R}}\Bigr),\qquad\frac{\partial D_{\mathrm{F}}}{\partial z_{v}}=\pi_{S}(v)-\pi_{T}(v). (4) Training moves z v z_{v} against its gradient. For a token the teacher prefers but the student almost never picks ( π S ​ ( v ) ≈ 0 \pi_{S}(v)\approx 0 ), the reverse-KL gradient carries the factor π S ​ ( v ) \pi_{S}(v) and barely moves it, while the forward-KL gradient is close to − π T ​ ( v ) -\pi_{T}(v) and raises it. A problems need behavior that has not appeared in the student’s responses, so we use forward KL. C problems only need to drop choices the teacher rejects, so we use reverse KL ( Jung et al., 2025 ) . This choice per stratum is the routing. This fixed-prefix argument only motivates the loss; it does not describe the gated update or guarantee a correct response ( Sheng et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Token cells and position selection.
sections.text: The token level (gating) works on a compressed teacher distribution. At each position we keep the teacher’s top K tok = 512 K_{\mathrm{tok}}=512 tokens plus one tail cell for the rest, indexed by j j in decreasing teacher probability. P t , j P_{t,j} and Q t , j Q_{t,j} are the teacher and student probabilities of cell j j at position t t . Both layers below select positions within a response. Let qt τ ⁡ ( u ) \operatorname{qt}_{\tau}(u) be the τ \tau -quantile of a score u u over the positions of one response (so long responses cannot take most selections); with τ = 0.8 \tau=0.8 , a position passes when its score is in the top 20% of its response.

sections.heading: 4.2  A Layer: Gated Forward KL
sections.text: Two kinds of positions help little on A problems. Where the student already matches the teacher, there is nothing to learn; where the teacher spreads its probability over many tokens, it cannot teach a definite choice. We measure disagreement by total variation TV t = 1 2 ​ ∑ j | P t , j − Q t , j | ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \mathrm{TV}_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}|P_{t,j}-Q_{t,j}|\in[0,1] , and teacher confidence by mass ​ @ ​ n ​ ( t ) = ∑ j = 1 n P t , j \mathrm{mass@}n(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}P_{t,j} , the probability the teacher puts on its top n n tokens. We keep a position only if both conditions hold, and the A loss averages the forward KL on the cells, D ( P t ∥ Q t ) = ∑ j P t , j log ( P t , j / Q t , j ) D(P_{t}\|Q_{t})=\sum_{j}P_{t,j}\log(P_{t,j}/Q_{t,j}) , over the kept positions: m t A = 𝟏 [ TV t ≥ qt τ ( TV ) ] ⋅ 𝟏 [ mass @ n ( t ) > 0.9 ] , ℒ A = ∑ t m A t D ( P t ∥ Q t ) ∑ t m t A . m^{A}_{t}=\mathbf{1}\bigl[\mathrm{TV}_{t}\geq\operatorname{qt}_{\tau}(\mathrm{TV})\bigr]\cdot\mathbf{1}\bigl[\mathrm{mass@}n(t)>0.9\bigr],\qquad\mathcal{L}^{A}=\frac{\sum_{t}m^{A}_{t}\,D(P_{t}\|Q_{t})}{\sum_{t}m^{A}_{t}}. (5) Here 𝟏 ​ [ ⋅ ] \mathbf{1}[\cdot] is 1 if the condition holds and 0 otherwise. The first condition keeps the 20% of positions with the largest disagreement. The second requires the teacher to put over 90% of its probability on a few candidates, that is, to be confident. We use r t r_{t} as a penalty: the larger r t r_{t} , the more we lower the probability of y t y_{t} . This needs only the student’s own response and no correctness reward ( Gu et al., 2024 ) (derivation in Appendix A.2 ). With ω t = − m t C ​ r t \omega_{t}=-m^{C}_{t}r_{t} held constant, the reverse-KL loss is ℒ RKL = − 1 | y | ∑ t ω t log π S ( y t ∣ s t ) . \mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{RKL}}=-\frac{1}{|y|}\textstyle\sum_{t}\omega_{t}\,\log\pi_{S}(y_{t}\mid s_{t}). (7) Unselected positions have ω t = 0 \omega_{t}=0 and are not updated.

sections.heading: Entropy brake.
sections.text: Reverse KL concentrates probability on a few tokens, which can remove other correct solutions and lower pass@ K K . Let H S ( t ) = − ∑ j Q t , j log Q t , j H_{S}(t)=-\sum_{j}Q_{t,j}\log Q_{t,j} and H T ( t ) = − ∑ j P t , j log P t , j H_{T}(t)=-\sum_{j}P_{t,j}\log P_{t,j} be the student and teacher entropies. Where H S − H T H_{S}-H_{T} is largest, reverse KL sharpens the student the most, so we raise the student entropy there, at positions picked by m t B m^{B}_{t} : m t B = 𝟏 [ H S ( t ) − H T ( t ) ≥ qt τ ( H S − H T ) ] , ℒ B = − β ∑ t m t B ​ H S ​ ( t ) ∑ t m t B . m^{B}_{t}=\mathbf{1}\bigl[H_{S}(t)-H_{T}(t)\geq\operatorname{qt}_{\tau}(H_{S}-H_{T})\bigr],\qquad\mathcal{L}^{B}=-\beta\,\frac{\sum_{t}m^{B}_{t}H_{S}(t)}{\sum_{t}m^{B}_{t}}. (8) We set β \beta once per pair before training so that the brake is about a tenth of the penalty in magnitude, a heuristic scale match rather than a gradient ratio, with 0.1 as a design choice (Appendix A.1 ).

sections.heading: Full objective and training loop.
sections.text: The C loss is ℒ C = ℒ RKL + ℒ B \mathcal{L}^{C}=\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{RKL}}+\mathcal{L}^{B} , and a response to problem x x uses the loss of its stratum: ℒ = ℒ A 1 [ x ∈ 𝒟 A ] + ℒ C 1 [ x ∈ 𝒟 C ] . \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}^{A}\,\mathbf{1}[x\in\mathcal{D}_{A}]+\mathcal{L}^{C}\,\mathbf{1}[x\in\mathcal{D}_{C}]. (9) Problems outside 𝒟 + \mathcal{D}_{+} give no loss. Each step, the student answers a batch of problems from 𝒟 + \mathcal{D}_{+} once, the teacher scores the answers, and we make one update; gates get no gradient (Algorithm 1 ). TS-OPD (routing only) removes gating by setting m t A ≡ m t C ≡ 1 m^{A}_{t}\equiv m^{C}_{t}\equiv 1 and β = 0 \beta=0 : ℒ A \mathcal{L}^{A} becomes forward KL averaged over all positions, and ℒ C \mathcal{L}^{C} becomes the sampled reverse KL on all positions.

sections.heading: Models and arms.
sections.text: The teachers are T 0 T_{0} (base-8B) and T 1 T_{1} (GRPO-8B); the students are Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . Every run trains for one epoch on the 7,496 MATH training problems ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) . Direct GRPO trains the same student with GRPO and no teacher; it is the S GRPO S_{\mathrm{GRPO}} that Section 3 sets out to beat. We compare it with OPD-r and OPD-f (uniform reverse and forward KL on all problems), and TS-OPD (routing only) and TS-OPD, which train on A ∪ \cup C only and so take about 91, 51, and 27 of the 118 OPD steps. Three controls, Direct GRPO (A ∪ \cup C), OPD-r (A ∪ \cup C), and OPD-f (A ∪ \cup C), use the same problems and steps as TS-OPD; only the loss differs. Details are in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Benchmarks and metrics.
sections.text: We sample K K responses per problem on eight benchmarks: MATH-test (5,000 problems, K = 1 K=1 ) and MATH500 ( K = 8 K=8 ) ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ; Lightman et al., 2023 ) , Minerva ( Lewkowycz et al., 2022 ) and OlympiadBench ( He et al., 2024 ) ( K = 8 K=8 ), and AIME24/25 ( Art of Problem Solving, n.d. ) and HMMT-Feb/Nov25 ( HMMT, 2025a ; HMMT, 2025b ) ( K = 16 K=16 ). We report macro avg@ K K and pass@ K K over all eight. sections.heading: 6  Conclusion
sections.text: Teacher improvement and student transfer are different objects. In mathematical reasoning, a GRPO-improved teacher can provide useful dense supervision, but only when OPD distinguishes acquisition gaps from consolidation gaps and avoids spending budget on no-gap or student-advantage problems. TS-OPD implements this transfer-aware view with problem-level routing, response-local token gates, and an entropy brake. Across two teacher lineages and three student sizes, the results show that the routed objective is most useful with a GRPO-improved teacher and that its gains depend on the full design. The broader lesson is that stronger teachers should be evaluated not only by endpoint accuracy, but by how their improvements decompose into teachable strata for the student.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Scope. All experiments use mathematical reasoning with verifiable answers, one model family (Qwen3), one teacher size (8B), and one RL algorithm (GRPO) for improving the teacher. The students go up to 4B. We have not tested whether the same strata and routing carry over to other domains, to students close to the teacher in size, or to teachers improved by other RL methods. Statistical strength. Most runs use a single training seed, so small differences may not be robust. We therefore read the per-problem outcome categories as trends rather than exact rates. Strata and budget. The strata come from K cal = 8 K_{\mathrm{cal}}=8 samples per training problem, taken once before training. With this budget, a problem with no observed student success may still be solvable, and a problem can move between strata as the student improves, but TS-OPD does not relabel it. Design choices and cost. The hyperparameter ablations use only the 0.6B student with the GRPO-8B teacher. Screening needs 2 ​ K cal 2K_{\mathrm{cal}} sampled responses per training problem before training, and every update needs the teacher’s top K tok K_{\mathrm{tok}} probabilities at each position. Finally, G transfer G_{\mathrm{transfer}} measures a gain shortfall; it does not isolate how much GRPO-acquired knowledge is lost (Section 3).

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.05974v1 [cs.LG] 05 Oct 2026 Transfer-Stratified On-Policy Distillation for RL-Improved Reasoning Teachers Xiaoyu Chen 1,2,∗ , Bo Shao 2 , Tiangang Zhu 2 , Bintao Wu 3 , Linjun Shou 2 , Fengge Wu 1 , Feng Sun 2 , Wenbiao Ding 2 1 Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences, 2 Microsoft, 3 Northwestern Polytechnical University ∗ Work done during an internship at Microsoft Reinforcement learning can substantially improve a reasoning teacher, but it is unclear which of those improvements survive when the teacher supervises a smaller on-policy student. We study this question in mathematical reasoning by comparing teacher lineages before and after GRPO, multiple student scales, direct GRPO, and several on-policy distillation objectives. The central finding is that transfer is structured rather than scalar: teacher strength alone does not make dense distillation competitive, while an RL-improved teacher creates useful but metric-dependent student gains. This motivates Transfer-Stratified On-Policy Distillation (TS-OPD), which screens training problems by the joint sampled success of the student and teacher, routes acquisition problems to gated forward KL, routes consolidation problems to gated reverse KL, and adds an entropy brake to protect sampled coverage. Across the main comparison, TS-OPD is the strongest student objective for macro average correctness with the GRPO-improved teacher, while pass@ K K remains more mixed. Ablations show that the gains come from routing and token gating rather than skipping problems. These results support a transfer-aware view of OPD: stronger teachers help when the supervision direction and token budget match the student’s observed ability, not merely because the teacher endpoint is stronger. Correspondence: Wenbiao Ding ( wenbiaoding@microsoft.com ) 1 Introduction On-policy distillation (OPD) is the dominant paradigm for transferring reasoning capabilities from large models to smaller ones ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . It trains students on their own generated states under token-level supervision from a frozen teacher, reducing the training–inference distribution mismatch. A teacher improved through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , should therefore provide stronger supervision. Prior work indeed shows that a GRPO-trained teacher produces a stronger student than the original teacher ( Xu et al., 2026b ) . Yet our initial observations on MATH ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) show that student gains can fall short of the teacher’s GRPO improvement. We call this shortfall the transfer gap and ask: which teacher improvements transfer to the student, which do not, and how can more of them be made to transfer? Our problem-level analysis on MATH shows that this gap is not uniform across training problems (Figure 1 ). Whether a teacher improvement can transfer depends on how the GRPO-trained teacher (hereafter, the GRPO teacher ) and student perform on each problem. Where the teacher outperforms the student, two distinct learning needs arise. If the student never solves the problem, it faces a knowledge gap : it needs guidance toward correct choices it has never explored, yet standard OPD supervises only its own responses, making such gains especially difficult to transfer. If the student solves the problem only sometimes, it faces a precision gap : it needs targeted correction of specific bad choices, whereas indiscriminate distillation may transfer only part of the gain or suppress correct behavior already acquired. Conversely, when the GRPO teacher does not outperform the student, it has little improvement to transfer. When their performance is comparable or both fail, the teacher offers no better direction; when the student is stronger, matching the teacher may be harmful. Standard OPD nevertheless supervises these problems uniformly. Skipping them concentrates the training budget on problems where transfer is possible. Figure 1: Overview of the transfer gap and its problem-level decomposition. Left: GRPO yields a teacher improvement Δ ​ T \Delta T , but standard OPD transfers only part of it into a student gain Δ ​ S \Delta S , leaving a transfer gap of Δ ​ T − Δ ​ S \Delta T-\Delta S . Middle: Joint teacher–student pass rates identify knowledge gaps (teacher > 0 >0 , student = 0 =0 ), precision gaps (teacher > > student > 0 >0 ), and problems with no transferable teacher advantage (teacher ≤ \leq student). Right: TS-OPD routes these three strata to matched actions—discover, refine, and skip, respectively. Existing OPD methods adapt supervision at the problem or token level ( Lin et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026c ; Xu et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Most closely related, Sparse-to-Dense distills from a GRPO-improved teacher using a common pipeline across problems ( Xu et al., 2026b ) . In contrast, we use the joint success of the teacher and raw student to identify each problem’s learning need and match both its KL direction and token-level supervision. We therefore propose Transfer-Stratified On-Policy Distillation (TS-OPD) . It first stratifies problems by the joint pass rates of the GRPO teacher and student, then routes knowledge and precision gaps to matched objectives with stratum-specific token gating, skipping problems without a teacher advantage. We evaluate TS-OPD across two teacher lineages (Qwen3-8B before and after GRPO), three student scales (0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B), four distillation objectives, and teacher-free direct GRPO. Our contributions are as follows: 1. We characterize and decompose the transfer gap in distillation from GRPO-improved teachers into distinct problem-level learning needs. 2. We propose TS-OPD , which stratifies and selects problems by observed teacher–student success, routes distillation objectives, and gates token-level supervision to address knowledge and precision gaps. 3. Experiments with a GRPO-improved teacher show that TS-OPD achieves the highest macro-average correctness and smallest benchmark-averaged transfer gap among evaluated methods at all three student scales, while distilling only on selected problems. 2 Related Work RL-improved teachers. DeepSeek-R1 distills an RL-trained model by fine-tuning on its responses ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . Sparse-to-Dense ( Xu et al., 2026b ) applies GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) to a larger teacher, then a forward-KL warmup and reverse-KL OPD uniformly across problems, and shows that the RL-improved teacher yields a student stronger than direct GRPO; it compares final students, not how much of the teacher’s GRPO gain is inherited, or where. Direct-OPD instead transfers the RL-induced policy shift, using the post-RL to pre-RL teacher log-ratio as a dense reward ( Feng et al., 2026 ) , while Li et al. (2026) find that OPD requires compatible thinking patterns and teacher capabilities new to the student ( Li et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2025 ) . On-policy objectives. GKD trains the student on its own samples and admits divergences beyond forward KL ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , and MiniLLM optimizes reverse KL on-policy ( Gu et al., 2024 ) . AKL, ToDi, EOPD, and TrOPD combine forward and reverse KL through adaptive weights, per-token probability ratios, teacher entropy, or token-level trust regions ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Jung et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2026 ; Xing et al., 2026 ) ; none chooses the direction from per-problem teacher and student performance ( Ko et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . Selective distillation. PACED weights each problem by p ⁡ ( 1 − p ) p(1-p) of the student pass rate p p and applies a forward-then-reverse KL schedule to all problems ( Xu et al., 2026a ) ; TREK applies forward KL on verified teacher proposals for prompts the student rarely solves, then returns to GRPO ( Xu et al., 2026d ; Yan et al., 2025 ) ; TGOPD routes each prompt to OPD or GRPO using verifier-scored teacher probes ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Within responses, OPDVR gates the distillation reward by trajectory correctness ( Lin et al., 2026 ) , and TIP selects tokens by student entropy and teacher–student divergence ( Xu et al., 2026c ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . Unlike these student-only or teacher-only signals, TS-OPD uses the joint success of the GRPO teacher and the raw student to choose each problem’s KL direction (forward for knowledge gaps, reverse for precision gaps) and adds response-local token gating, rather than introducing problem-level selection itself. 3 Problem Definition and Transfer-Gap Diagnosis Building on our observations on MATH, we formalize the transfer gap and identify knowledge and precision gaps on MATH training problems. We examine these strata alongside gain shortfalls on held-out competition benchmarks to motivate differentiated OPD supervision. 3.1 Evaluation Metrics and the GRPO Transfer Gap For each problem x i x_{i} , we sample K K responses from model M M under fixed decoding settings and score them with a verifier c i ​ ( y ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } c_{i}(y)\in\{0,1\} . The sampled success rate is p ^ M , i = K − 1 ​ ∑ j = 1 K c i ​ ( y M , i , j ) \widehat{p}_{M,i}=K^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{K}c_{i}(y_{M,i,j}) . With test accuracy a ⁡ ( M ) = 100 ​ avg ​ @ ⁡ K ​ ( M ) a(M)=100\operatorname{avg@}K(M) , define the teacher and student gains and the transfer gap : Δ T = a ⁡ ( T 1 ) − a ⁡ ( T 0 ) , Δ S = a ⁡ ( S OPD ) − a ⁡ ( S 0 ) , G transfer = Δ T − Δ S . \Delta_{T}=a(T_{1})-a(T_{0}),\qquad\Delta_{S}=a(S_{\mathrm{OPD}})-a(S_{0}),\qquad G_{\mathrm{transfer}}=\Delta_{T}-\Delta_{S}. It may include knowledge already present in T 0 T_{0} , so the gap does not isolate the loss of GRPO-acquired knowledge. With the teacher and student initialization fixed, our goal is to reduce this gap and outperform S GRPO S_{\mathrm{GRPO}} , trained directly with GRPO from the same S 0 S_{0} . 3.2 Two Learning Gaps on Training Problems We hypothesize that incomplete transfer partly reflects supervision mismatched to problem-specific learning needs . A stronger teacher need not outperform the student on every problem. Where it does, the guidance needed depends on whether the student can already generate a correct response. Before distillation, we therefore sample K cal = 8 K_{\mathrm{cal}}=8 responses per training problem from both T 1 T_{1} and S 0 S_{0} and classify their joint success rates. Because OPD queries the teacher along student-generated prefixes ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) , guidance along complete correct solutions may be limited. Feedback at incorrect prefixes remains available but may not suffice to reach a correct solution, motivating guidance toward teacher-preferred continuations the student rarely selects. For C, uniform supervision may miss decisive errors and spend limited budget on P and N, leaving learnable problems undertrained. This motivates targeted correction while preserving existing correct behavior. These mechanism hypotheses require fixed-budget stratification controls and token-level analysis. We therefore prioritize A and C with supervision matched to knowledge acquisition and precision improvement, deferring teacher matching on P and N. Strata are assigned before training from joint teacher–student samples; rollouts remain student-generated. 4 Transfer-Stratified On-Policy Distillation TS-OPD labels training problems by the teacher and student success observed before training and works at two levels (Figure 2 ). At the problem level , it trains only on A and C problems ( filtering ) and applies forward KL to A and reverse KL to C ( routing ). At the token level , it updates only selected positions within each response and adds an entropy brake on C ( gating ). In mathematical reasoning, a GRPO-improved teacher can provide useful dense supervision, but only when OPD distinguishes acquisition gaps from consolidation gaps and avoids spending budget on no-gap or student-advantage problems. TS-OPD implements this transfer-aware view with problem-level routing, response-local token gates, and an entropy brake. Across two teacher lineages and three student sizes, the results show that the routed objective is most useful with a GRPO-improved teacher and that its gains depend on the full design. The broader lesson is that stronger teachers should be evaluated not only by endpoint accuracy, but by how their improvements decompose into teachable strata for the student. Limitations Scope. All experiments use mathematical reasoning with verifiable answers, one model family (Qwen3), one teacher size (8B), and one RL algorithm (GRPO) for improving the teacher. The students go up to 4B. We have not tested whether the same strata and routing carry over to other domains, to students close to the teacher in size, or to teachers improved by other RL methods. Statistical strength. Most runs use a single training seed, so small differences may not be robust. We therefore read the per-problem outcome categories as trends rather than exact rates. Strata and budget. The strata come from K cal = 8 K_{\mathrm{cal}}=8 samples per training problem, taken once before training. With this budget, a problem with no observed student success may still be solvable, and a problem can move between strata as the student improves, but TS-OPD does not relabel it. Design choices and cost. The hyperparameter ablations use only the 0.6B student with the GRPO-8B teacher. Screening needs 2 ​ K cal 2K_{\mathrm{cal}} sampled responses per training problem before training, and every update needs the teacher’s top K tok K_{\mathrm{tok}} probabilities at each position. Finally, G transfer G_{\mathrm{transfer}} measures a gain shortfall; it does not isolate how much GRPO-acquired knowledge is lost (Section 3). References Agarwal et al.
